newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia to consider media rule changes.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia to consider media rule changes.

text.p: The Australian government said on Tuesday that it would release an issues paper on possible changes to the rules governing ownership of the nation's electronic media and newspapers.
Communications Minister Richard Alston said there would be an extensive public consultation period before legislation was introduced into parliament in the New Year.
"Submissions on the issues paper will inform the release of a draft exposure bill which will also be available for public scrutiny prior to parliamentary debate," Alston said.
The government policy paper is an alternative to a full public inquiry into media ownership rules.
The Liberal-National government said before the March 2 election that it planned to hold a full inquiry into media ownership rules laid down by the former Labor government.

Alston said the government would consider the effectiveness of current rules, the extent to which media specific regulation was necessary, the implications of the emergence of new communications technologies and services, and level of government intervention.
It would also consider the impact of changes to cross media rules on foreign ownership and control arrangements, he said.
The current rules stop foreign investors from owning more than 25 percent of a newspaper group or 15 percent of a television group, but allows foreigners unlimited access to radio.
The rules also stop local companies from owning both a television company and a newspaper group in the same city.

Most commentary about the planned media inquiry and the government's likely free-market attitude to the industry has centred on the Fairfax newspaper group which has a share register full of local and overseas media barons keen to snare control of the company and its healthy advertising revenue in Sydney and Melbourne.
Recent media reports said the government could not agree on a suitable candidate as chairman of the media inquiry, although Alston said he had a name firmly in mind.

Canadian media proprietor Conrad Black, who owns 25 percent of John Fairfax Holdings Ltd FXJ AX, has repeatedly said he wanted government permission to increase his stake to at least 35 percent, thus ensuring some protection from his media rivals.
Black, the owner of United States and Canadian publishing group Hollinger Inc HLR.N as well as London's Telegraph Plc, has also indicated he may sell his stake if permission is not granted.

Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd has a stake of under five percent in Fairfax and already controls more than 70 percent of the nation's metropolitan newspaper market with papers and presses in each state capital.
Murdoch also owns 15 percent of the Seven Network Ltd, the maximum he is allowed without government permission.

Kerry Packer's Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd which wholly owns the leading Nine television network, has a stake of just under 15 percent in Fairfax and has said it eventually wanted the two companies to merge their operations.
